---
title: "Reference selection"
subtitle: "Module 2 — 30 min"
---

## Why it matters

Reads are mapped to **one** reference, and the consensus is built from that mapping. A reference that is too divergent makes reads map badly (or not at all), hides real variants and **biases the consensus towards the reference**.

| Criterion                   | Question                                                      |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Same species / lineage      | is it the right virus, the right lineage?                     |
| Close to your samples       | fewer differences = better mapping                            |
| Complete and good quality   | complete genome, few ambiguous bases (N)                      |
| Well documented             | accession number, host, country, collection date              |
| Consistent across the study | the **same** reference for all the samples you compare        |

## Step 1 — Download three candidate references from NCBI

Since the mapping exercise you have used **NC_045512.2** (Wuhan-Hu-1), the RefSeq reference of SARS-CoV-2. Where does it come from, and is it the only possible choice? Download it again, together with two other viruses, directly from NCBI:

```bash
mkdir -p data/ncbi/candidates
efetch -db nuccore -id NC_045512.2 -format fasta > data/ncbi/candidates/SARS-CoV-2_NC_045512.2.fasta
efetch -db nuccore -id MN996532.2  -format fasta > data/ncbi/candidates/RaTG13_MN996532.2.fasta
efetch -db nuccore -id NC_004718.3 -format fasta > data/ncbi/candidates/SARS-CoV-1_NC_004718.3.fasta
```

(Plan B without `efetch`: search the accession on <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore>, then **Send to → Complete record → File → FASTA**.)

```bash
seqkit stats data/ncbi/candidates/*.fasta
```

- `NC_045512.2`: SARS-CoV-2, the reference used in this course;
- `MN996532.2` (RaTG13): a bat coronavirus, roughly 96 % identical to SARS-CoV-2;
- `NC_004718.3`: SARS-CoV-1, another virus, roughly 80 % identical.

**Questions:** what are the lengths of the three genomes? Which one is the same species as your sample?

## Step 2 — Which candidate is closest to your sample?

Use a subset of the trimmed reads from the previous exercises (100,000 read pairs is enough) and map it to each candidate:

```bash
mkdir -p results/ref_test
seqkit head -n 100000 results/trimmed/SRR26396743_1_paired.fastq.gz -o results/ref_test/sub_1.fastq.gz
seqkit head -n 100000 results/trimmed/SRR26396743_2_paired.fastq.gz -o results/ref_test/sub_2.fastq.gz
```

```bash
for ref in SARS-CoV-2_NC_045512.2 RaTG13_MN996532.2 SARS-CoV-1_NC_004718.3; do
  bwa index data/ncbi/candidates/$ref.fasta 2> /dev/null
  echo "== $ref"
  bwa mem -t 2 data/ncbi/candidates/$ref.fasta results/ref_test/sub_1.fastq.gz results/ref_test/sub_2.fastq.gz 2> /dev/null \
    | samtools flagstat - | grep -E "in total|mapped \("
done
```

**Questions**

1. Which reference gives the highest percentage of mapped reads?
2. What happens with RaTG13? With SARS-CoV-1?
3. What would this change in the consensus (think of IGV and of Step 5 of the consensus exercise)?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
Use the values from your own run. You should see that the SARS-CoV-2 reference maps the most reads and that the other viruses map fewer, with the most distant one the worst. With about 4 % divergence (RaTG13) a 150-base read already carries several mismatches; with about 20 % (SARS-CoV-1) most reads cannot be placed. Reads that do map to a divergent reference carry many false differences, and the consensus becomes biased towards the reference. The lesson: **check that the reference is close to your virus before mapping**.
:::

## Step 3 — Download references of several lineages from NCBI Virus

To place your genome in a tree (next sessions), we need **reference genomes of several lineages**, from the same database. Open NCBI Virus: <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/labs/virus> and choose **SARS-CoV-2** (taxid 2697049).

1. In the filters on the left, keep **Nucleotide completeness: complete** and **Host: *Homo sapiens***.
2. Filter by **Pango lineage** (or add the lineage column to the table with *Customize columns*) and choose **one or two genomes per lineage**.
3. Choose lineages that span the pandemic: the ancestral lineage **B** (Wuhan-Hu-1, accession NC_045512.2), Alpha (B.1.1.7), Delta (B.1.617.2), Omicron (BA.1, BA.2, BA.5) **and the lineages circulating when your sample was collected** (look at the `collection_date` of the run `SRR26396743` on its NCBI BioSample page).
4. Prefer genomes with a full date and country, and with few ambiguous bases.
5. Select about 10–15 genomes, then **Download → Nucleotide → FASTA → Build custom**, and put **Accession** and **Pango lineage** in the definition line. Save the file as `data/ncbi/lineage_refs.fasta`.

Clean the names (no spaces, no `|`: the tree software does not like them):

```bash
sed '/^>/ { s/[ |][ |]*/_/g; s/_$// }' data/ncbi/lineage_refs.fasta > data/ncbi/lineage_refs.clean.fasta
grep '>' data/ncbi/lineage_refs.clean.fasta
```

Each name should now look like `ACCESSION_LINEAGE`. Check that `NC_045512.2` is in the list: it will be our root.

**Questions:** how many genomes did you keep? Which criteria did you use to choose them?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
The criteria are the table at the top of the page: same species, complete genome, few `N`, documented (accession, lineage, date, country), and a good spread of lineages and dates so that the tree has meaningful comparisons. One genome per lineage is enough for this exercise; real studies use many more.
:::

## Final question

Why should all the samples of a study be mapped to the **same** reference?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
Because differences are measured **against the reference**, with its coordinates. If each sample used another reference, positions would not correspond, mutations would not be comparable, and differences between references would be mistaken for differences between samples. One common reference = one common coordinate system = genomes you can align and compare.
:::
